# OpenBot **OpenBot is a self-hostable workspace for AI coworkers.** Give a Bot a job, connect the tools it needs, and work with it on your own machine or across your team. You can create a Bot in OpenBot or bring an agent you already run through AG-UI. A Bot can use a browser, work with files, and call the tools you grant it. You can watch it work, take over to sign in, and hand the browser back. Bring any AG-UI agent, written on a framework or by hand, and it arrives as a coworker with a channel of its own. Watch it work on its own screen, take the wheel when it reaches something it should not do alone, then hand it back. It answers with components rather than only prose, and the whole thing runs on your own machine.
You can get started with OpenBot in three ways. - **Use the open-source template.** Clone the MIT-licensed application and make it your own. Replace the example tenant package under `examples/` with your own coworkers, channels, and skills. The [quick start](#quick-start) runs the template from source. - **Download Personal Edition.** Choose your installer for [Mac (Apple silicon)](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-mac-arm64.dmg), [Mac (Intel)](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-mac-x64.dmg), or [Windows (x64)](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-windows-x64-setup.exe). The desktop app runs the workspace and CopilotKit Intelligence locally on your computer. Connect your model and start with the built-in Personal Assistant. Your model provider bills for usage separately. - **OpenBot for Business.** Deploy on your infrastructure with the [Helm chart](charts/openbot/README.md) or have CopilotKit host your workspace. Both options are in [early access](https://openbot.co/business). Our engineers can help you deploy and customize OpenBot for your team. [**Start the conversation**](https://copilotkit.ai/talk-to-an-engineer?ref=openbot_readme). ## What it is In Personal Edition, you start with one assistant on your computer. With the source template, Docker Compose starts the supporting services, PostgreSQL stores the workspace configuration, and you choose the model. OpenBot encrypts stored model credentials and keeps them out of logs. The team template comes with two Bots. **General Assistant** helps with everyday work. **Knowledge** answers questions from the company documents you connect and cites its sources. To add a Bot, open `/bots` or start from one of the [YAML examples](examples/fintech/catalog/). For example, [Meeting Follow-ups](examples/fintech/catalog/meeting-follow-ups.yaml) reads meeting notes and lists who agreed to do what. Copy its file into `examples/fintech/agents/` and restart OpenBot to try it. You grant tool access separately, so you can let a Bot read a document without giving it permission to edit it. More at [openbot.co](https://openbot.co). ## Built on AG-UI A Bot is any endpoint speaking [AG-UI](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui), the open protocol for agent-to-user interaction, so OpenBot is not tied to a framework and neither are you. Agents built with LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or written by hand all arrive the same way, and the governance rides the protocol rather than the framework. ## Requirements To run the open-source template locally, you’ll need the following. - Docker, for PostgreSQL and the shipped Bots. - [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4+, for the app, the API server and the tests (some tests fail on 1.3). - A CopilotKit Intelligence project and license. A free plan is available, and Intelligence can be self-hosted. - A model key. The proof-of-concept Bot uses OpenAI; the LangGraph Bot can use OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. ## Quick start The example configuration sets `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true`, so you can try the app as a local administrator. Configure [sign-in](#sign-in) before giving anyone else access. On a Mac, the free Developer plan also covers [running Intelligence locally](#intelligence-on-your-own-machine) with Docker. > **Setting up with an AI assistant?** Paste [`prompt.txt`](prompt.txt) into it first. It carries the > same steps as below plus the things that are easy to get wrong: which of the blank keys in > `.env.example` are actually yours to fill (the CopilotKit key and a model key), which the start > script fills for you, and what each start-up refusal means. Every claim in it is checked against > this repository. 1. Create `.env`: ```sh cp .env.example .env bun install ``` 2. Connect a fresh managed Intelligence project: ```sh npx --yes copilotkit@latest login npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select bun scripts/setup-learning.ts ``` The helper provisions the selected project's runtime key, creates or reuses its `openbot` Learning container, then writes both settings to `.env`. It preserves custom container assignments and never replaces an existing OpenBot key; with one set, it only creates `openbot` in that key's project if it is missing. For fresh self-hosted setup, set `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL` to that deployment's HTTPS API origin (or `http://localhost` for a local one) and run the helper without the two `npx` commands. It opens an isolated Chrome or Edge window for your usual sign-in and project choice; install either browser first. For CLI-managed local evaluation installs, it discovers the matching dashboard with the newest installed or cached CopilotKit CLI and uses that dashboard for login and session requests. Discovery runs offline with Bun, without downloading the CLI or requiring `npx` on your PATH. If no CLI is available, manually hosted deployments use their API origin for sign-in. Complete the local auth approval shown in the browser when prompted. The runtime API URL stays unchanged. It writes the API URL, the key and the container, not `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL`, so set that one to the same deployment yourself. Once `openbot` exists, the server assigns it as the default by itself unless [Admin → Automatic Learning](docs/automatic-learning.md) has a saved setting. Managed Intelligence needs no separate licence token. The same CopilotKit CLI sign-in provisions Composio automatically when you run `bash scripts/start.sh`. If that cannot complete, OpenBot still starts, with apps unavailable. You can run `bun run setup:composio` first to prepare it separately, or later to retry; it does not need a Learning container. The helper creates or reuses one isolated Composio project for this installation and saves its project key to `.env`. Existing Composio keys and Arcade configurations are preserved. Keep the private `.env.openbot-installation-id` file across restarts and interrupted setup attempts; do not copy it into a new installation. This needs a published CopilotKit CLI with `integrations composio provision` and the hosted provisioning service enabled. See [Composio setup](docs/plugins/composio.md#automatic-project-setup) for deployment preparation. 3. Fill the remaining required values: - `OPENAI_API_KEY` Keep the managed Intelligence URLs from `.env.example` unless you run Intelligence yourself. The example `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is public and fine locally; generate your own with: ```sh openssl rand -base64 32 ``` 4. Run: ```sh bash scripts/start.sh ``` 5. Open . `scripts/start.sh` starts Docker services, applies migrations, starts the API server on port 3001, starts the routine worker, starts the app on port 3010, and checks that the services answer their own health routes before printing next steps. `scripts/stop.sh` takes the same things down, including each Bot's computer, which compose does not own; `--keep-computers` leaves the computers running. Nothing is deleted: the database, the Bots' files and their browser profiles are volumes. ### On Windows Run the clone inside WSL 2 with Ubuntu, and run every step above from an Ubuntu terminal. [Windows (WSL 2)](docs/development.md#windows-wsl-2) lists what to install in Ubuntu first. Keep an Ubuntu terminal open while you use OpenBot, and open the app from your Windows browser at . ### Intelligence on your own machine To try Intelligence on one Mac instead of the managed service, follow [Evaluate Intelligence locally](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/intelligence/self-hosting-local). The free [Developer plan](https://www.copilotkit.ai/pricing) qualifies. The local licence lasts 30 days and `npx copilotkit@latest local renew` renews it as often as you need, while your account is in good standing. It is a preview for macOS with Docker Desktop, not a production installation. Run its `npx copilotkit@latest local connect` from the OpenBot root, where `.env` is. That command writes `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL`, `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL` and `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY` to `.env`. OpenBot reads those settings directly; no key copying or renaming is needed. `INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY` remains supported for older configurations. When both are set, the non-empty CLI key takes precedence so reconnecting uses the new project's key. To give the Bots a Learning container on that stack, see [Automatic Learning](docs/automatic-learning.md). ## Deploy it One image carries the app, the API, the browser the Bots drive, and optionally PostgreSQL. Same `.env`, no Kubernetes. ```sh # The published image. Nothing to clone and nothing to build. docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \ -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql \ ghcr.io/copilotkit/openbot:latest # Or the tree you have in front of you. docker build -t openbot . docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \ -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql openbot ``` Everything is on 3001 here, the app included, rather than the 3010 the clone uses. `latest` is the most recent release and a version tag such as `:v0.0.9` pins one. Leave `EMBEDDED_POSTGRES` off and set `DATABASE_URL` to point at a database you already run. [docs/deployment.md](docs/deployment.md) has the minimum sizes, the platform notes, and how it behaves behind more than one replica. ## Try it Pick a task you know well enough to review. For example, ask a Bot to check a hotel receipt against a travel policy in Drive. Have it show the room rate and tax separately so you can decide whether the claim meets the nightly limit. Use **Teach a Bot** to record the steps you want it to follow on the next claim. - Open `/bot` and ask: `Open news.ycombinator.com and tell me the top story.` - Ask the Bot to fill out , then inspect `/admin/audit`. - Open `/admin/boundaries`, add a deny rule or preset, and retry the same browser action. - Create a Bot from `/bots`, give it a standing role, and start a channel with it. ## Main `/admin/audit` | Review permitted, refused, and failed actions. | ## Features - **A computer per person**: the supervisor gives each person their own container, with a folder and browser profile for each of their Bots. Tick Isolated on a Bot to give it a container of its own. Set `COMPUTER_RUNTIME=runsc` to run them under gVisor where the host supports it. - **A shell, not just a browser**: a Bot can run a command in its workspace, install what it needs, and process a file it saved. Through the same gate as everything else, so a rule can refuse a shell outright or refuse particular commands, and the command is on the record either way. The command inherits PATH, locale, terminal and proxy variables, not the rest of the deployment's environment. - **The gateway is the only way in**: it resolves the target from a server-held snapshot, evaluates the policy, writes the audit row, and only then calls the computer. There is no path that acts without the record existing first. - **CEL policy, fail closed**: rules can inspect `tool.name`, `intent`, `bot.id`, `actor.id`, `page.url`, `page.host`, `element.*`, `key`, `command`, `file.*`, `mcp.*` and `initiator.*` (what started the run, so a rule can refuse a scheduled routine what it would allow a person). Deny is evaluated before allow, a missing policy permits nothing, and a broken rule refuses rather than opens. - **Watch what it is doing**: the screen shows what a Bot is looking at, and the Activity list under it shows what it ran, read and saved in this conversation, with the output. A command line in the transcript opens to the same thing. A saved file shows its path and size, never its contents. - **Take the wheel**: a Bot that hits a login wall or a 2FA prompt asks for help.
